passages.t: ‘So that I may dwell among them’
passages.happening:
“Tell the Israelites to bring Me an offering. You are to receive My offering from every man whose heart compels him” (verse 2).

The gifts are listed: gold, silver and bronze; blue, purple and scarlet yarn; fine linen and goat hair; dyed ram skins and fine leather; acacia wood; oil, spices, and precious stones (verses 3-7).

“And they are to make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them. You must make the tabernacle and design all its furnishings according to the pattern I show you” (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
Moses has gone into the cloud on the mountain (24:18). What God gives him first is not more law. It is a building plan.

The rest of the book has a clear shape. Chapters 25 to 31 give the instructions for the tabernacle. Chapters 35 to 40 tell how it was built. Between them stands the golden calf (32 to 34), the people's attempt to make a god they could see.

Verse 8 gives the purpose of the whole plan: ‘so that I may dwell among them’. The exodus did not end at the sea, or even at Sinai. Its goal was God living in the middle of his people's camp. The Hebrew word for the tabernacle, mishkan, means a dwelling place. It is not a place Israel goes to visit God. It is where God lives among Israel.

The gifts are freely given, from everyone ‘whose heart compels him’. The list reads like a list of the costliest things of the ancient world. Blue and purple dye came from sea snails gathered along the coast of Phoenicia. Scarlet came from a small insect. Acacia is a hard, lasting tree of the desert, one of the few timbers to be had there. The word behind ‘fine leather’ is uncertain.

Everything must follow ‘the pattern I show you’. The Hebrew word, tavnit, means a plan or model. Whether Moses saw a heavenly original, a model, or plans in a vision, the text does not say.

The instructions begin at the center, with the ark in the innermost room, and work outward. That is the order of holiness, not the order of building.

The New Testament draws some lines from the tabernacle to Christ, and those lines are given below where Scripture draws them. Readers have sometimes found a hidden meaning in every board and peg. These notes do not. The tent first meant what it says: God came to live with his people.
passages.later:
Hebrews quotes the command about the pattern and calls the tabernacle “a copy and shadow of what is in heaven” (Hebrews 8:5). A shadow is real. It has the shape of what casts it. It is not the thing itself.

John writes, “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory” (John 1:14). The Greek verb for ‘made His dwelling’ is built on the word for a tent. God's dwelling among his people now has a human face.

Paul says of giving, “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
passages.hard:
Why would the God of heaven need a tent to live in?

The chapter says plainly that the sanctuary exists so that God may dwell among his people. Yet Solomon, at the temple, confesses, “Even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built” (1 Kings 8:27), and Stephen says, “the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands” (Acts 7:48).

Scripture holds both together. Israel's neighbors believed a god lived in his statue and needed feeding and care. Israel's sanctuary had no image at all. God is present there without being shut in or managed. Some interpreters stress that the presence was real: God truly chose to be near in one place, and his glory really filled the tent. Others stress that God stooped to meet a people who needed a sign of his nearness. The two fit together. The tent met Israel's need, not God's, and it pointed to a fuller dwelling still to come.
passages.asks: God asked for gifts only from those whose hearts moved them. Ask what you give to God gladly, and what you give only because you must. And ask what it means to you that God's great aim was not only to rescue his people but to live among them.

passages.t: The ark and the mercy seat
passages.happening:
“And they are to construct an ark of acacia wood, two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and a cubit and a half high” (verse 10). It is covered with gold inside and out, with rings and poles to carry it (verses 11-14). “The poles are to remain in the rings of the ark; they must not be removed” (verse 15). Inside it goes “the Testimony, which I will give you” (verse 16).

On top is “a mercy seat of pure gold” (verse 17), with two cherubim of hammered gold at its ends, wings spread over it, facing each other (verses 18-20).

“And I will meet with you there above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim that are over the ark of the Testimony” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The ark is a chest. A cubit was the length of a forearm, about 18 inches or 45 centimeters, so the ark was roughly 3.75 feet long and 2.25 feet wide and high, about 1.1 by 0.7 by 0.7 meters. Inside went ‘the Testimony’, the stone tablets of the covenant.

The poles never came out. The ark was always ready to travel.

The lid is the mercy seat, kapporet in Hebrew. The word is related to the verb for making atonement, which is why many Bibles call it the atonement cover. Over it stood two cherubim, winged guardians.

People in Israel's world knew pictures of kings and gods seated on thrones between winged creatures. The stone coffin of Ahiram, a king of Byblos, shows a throne with winged sphinxes on each side. Egyptian craftsmen made gilded chests and shrines carried on poles; one was found in the tomb of Tutankhamun. The ark belongs to that world, with one great difference. No figure sits on the throne. The LORD is the King no one can see, enthroned above the cherubim, and the ark is his footstool.

And here God promises to meet Moses and to speak. The center of Israel's worship was not a statue. It was an empty throne above a chest holding God's words.
passages.later:
The psalms praise God as the King “enthroned above the cherubim” (Psalm 99:1), and David calls the ark “a footstool for our God” (1 Chronicles 28:2).

Hebrews describes the inner room: “the gold-covered ark of the covenant”, and “Above the ark were the cherubim of glory, overshadowing the mercy seat” (Hebrews 9:4-5).

The Greek Old Testament called the mercy seat hilasterion. Paul uses that word when he writes that “God presented Him as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood” (Romans 3:25). The place of atonement is now a person.

The ark was later lost, most likely when Babylon took Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC. Jeremiah had looked ahead to a day when “no one will remember it or miss it” (Jeremiah 3:16).
passages.asks: At the heart of the tabernacle was God's word and a place of mercy, and God promised to speak there. Ask where you expect to meet God, and whether you come expecting him to speak. And ask what it means to you that the meeting place is called the mercy seat.

passages.happening:
“You are also to make a table of acacia wood two cubits long, a cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high” (verse 23). It is covered with gold, with a rim and rings and poles (verses 24-28). Its plates, dishes, pitchers and bowls are of pure gold (verse 29).

“And place the Bread of the Presence on the table before Me at all times” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
The table stood in the outer room of the tent. On it lay the Bread of the Presence: twelve loaves, the number of Israel's tribes, renewed every Sabbath, set before God as a sign of the covenant, and then eaten by the priests.

In neighboring temples, meals were set before the statue of a god, as if the god ate them. Israel's God had no statue to feed. The bread was not food for God. Twelve loaves for twelve tribes lay always ‘before Me’, in his presence.
passages.later:
Leviticus gives the rule: “Every Sabbath day the bread is to be set out before the LORD on behalf of the Israelites as a permanent covenant” (Leviticus 24:8).

Jesus said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). He does not point to this table when he says it, so the link is one of theme: God is the one who gives his people bread.
passages.asks: Twelve loaves lay before God at all times, set out on behalf of the whole people. Ask whom you hold before God, and whom you have forgotten. And ask whether you believe you are kept in God's presence even when you do not feel it.

passages.happening:
“Then you are to make a lampstand of pure, hammered gold. It shall be made of one piece, including its base and shaft, its cups, and its buds and petals” (verse 31). It has six branches, three on each side, with cups “shaped like almond blossoms” (verses 32-36).

“Make seven lamps and set them up on the lampstand so that they illuminate the area in front of it” (verse 37). It is made from a talent of pure gold (verse 39).

“See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
The lampstand is shaped like a flowering almond tree, with branches, buds and blossoms, all hammered from one piece of gold. A talent of gold weighed about 75 pounds, or 34 kilograms, though the weight of a talent varied.

Its seven lamps lit the holy place where the priests served.

Many readers have noticed that the tabernacle carries echoes of Eden. Gold and onyx were found in the land near the garden. Cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life. And here is a lamp shaped like a tree, burning in God's presence. On this reading, the tent is a small picture of the garden where God once walked with his people.

The chapter ends as it began, with the pattern shown on the mountain.
passages.later:
Genesis says of the land by Eden, “the gold of that land is pure, and bdellium and onyx are found there” (Genesis 2:12), and that God “stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden” (Genesis 3:24).

In Revelation the risen Christ stands among seven golden lampstands, and he explains them: “the seven lampstands are the seven churches” (Revelation 1:20).

Jesus said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). As with the bread, he does not point to the lampstand, so the link is one of theme.
passages.asks: The lamp burned in God's presence so that the priests could serve. Ask what light you need for the work God has given you. And ask whether your life gives light to those around you, as the churches in Revelation were meant to.
